text:
A: Hello? Can you hear me alright?
B: Yeah, yeah, I can hear you. Hi, I'm Isaac.
A: Haider. Nice one. You alright?
B: Yeah, good, good. Bit knackered, had a nine o'clock this morning, so, erm, yeah. Running on fumes, kind of.
A: Nine o'clock lecture, that's rough. What you studying?
B: Economics, at City. Second year. So it's like, train from Thornton Heath into London Bridge, then the Tube, and Southern are just... they're never on time, honestly. Today it was twenty minutes late and I'm just standing there on the platform like, I've got a seminar, you know.
A: Southern, yeah. I'm out west, Hanwell, so I've got the 207, which is basically the same experience but on a bus. You just accept it after a while.
B: Ha, yeah. Sorry, what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
A: No, course. I'm IT at a college in west London. Network, Wi-Fi, the projectors in the classrooms, all that. Basically if a teacher's screen goes blank, I'm the guy that walks in.
B: Oh, that makes sense actually, 'cause I saw the cables on your shelf in the photo. And the book. CCNP, is it?
A: Yeah, the CCNP. That book's been on that shelf for over a year, to be fair. It's more of a decoration at this point.
B: Ha, no, I get that. I've got a stack of finance books I keep saying I'll read over summer.
A: How'd you find the puzzle thing at the start, by the way?
B: Erm, I think I did alright? I don't know, the last couple I was kind of guessing. Did you finish it?
A: Nah, I ran out of time on the last one. Wasn't stressing though. It'll be fine.
B: Yeah, true, true. I always get a bit, like, tense with timed stuff, sorry, I'm rambling.
A: You're good, mate. Take your time. You play football? I saw the Palace scarf.
B: Yeah, Palace, through my dad mostly. I play five-a-side most Wednesdays with my old school mates. And I saw your Chelsea scarf, so, I won't hold it against you.
A: Ha, appreciate that. Wednesdays, yeah, I used to play Wednesdays in Acton, about ten years. Then my back went, a disc thing, two years ago, so now I just watch. Walk the canal instead, like an old man.
B: Ah, that's bad, sorry. Is it alright now, like, day to day?
A: Mostly. If I sit in the car too long it plays up. The physio gave me exercises and I do them when I remember, which is, you know, not often. Thirty-four and I've got a dodgy back. My mum thinks it's hilarious.
B: Nah, that's not old, man. My dad's in his fifties and he still plays, he just complains for about three days after.
A: That's the spirit, to be fair. What d'you wanna do after uni then, with the economics?
B: Erm, ideally like a grad scheme in the City, banking or consulting. I'm applying for spring weeks and stuff now. It's kind of competitive though, so I've got a spreadsheet of all the deadlines and, yeah. Trying to get ahead of it, you know.
A: A spreadsheet, that's organised. You're more organised than my whole office.
B: Ha, I try. It's mainly 'cause I panic if I don't, if I'm honest.
A: Nah, that's sensible. You remind me of my little brother a bit, actually. He's got a list for everything as well.
B: Is he older or younger than me?
A: He's twenty-nine, works in a pharmacy. We just play FIFA together most nights and argue about it.
B: Ha, that's the same with me and my sister but with chargers, she keeps nicking mine.
A: Classic. My niece and nephew wreck my controllers every Sunday, so—
